questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Separation of powers as a design choice
questions.learningObjective: Explain separation of powers as a design choice
questions.stem: A train dispatcher's log notes that powers are split among branches to prevent concentration.

options.text: Separation of powers divides authority to prevent any single branch dominating.
Separation of powers aims to concentrate authority in one branch.
Separation of powers eliminates checks between branches.
Separation of powers applies only during emergencies.

questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides authority to prevent concentration. The tempting error is to confuse separation with total independence.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks why the United States has two court systems.

answer.exemplar: The United States has two court systems because federal courts handle federal questions and state courts handle state law, reflecting divided sovereignty under the Constitution.

questions.explanation: Federal and state courts coexist because sovereignty is divided. The tempting error is to assume one system suffices.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Trial and appellate courts by purpose

stimulus.body: A trial court hears evidence and finds facts, while an appellate court reviews legal errors without reweighing evidence. The dispatcher log must classify a court's role.

questions.stem: Which court finds facts and hears evidence?

options.text: The appellate court finds facts and hears new evidence.
Both courts find facts equally.
The trial court finds facts and hears evidence.
Neither court finds facts.

questions.explanation: Trial courts find facts and hear evidence, while appellate courts review law. The tempting error is to reverse these roles.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the constitution fixes about the Supreme Court
questions.learningObjective: Recall constitutional features of the Supreme Court

stimulus.body: The Constitution fixes the existence of a Supreme Court and its original jurisdiction, while leaving details like size to Congress. The dispatcher log reviews this rule.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Supreme Court is fixed by the Constitution?

options.text: The number of justices is fixed at nine by the Constitution.
The retirement age of justices is fixed by the Constitution.
The size of each circuit is fixed by the Constitution.
The existence of a Supreme Court is fixed by the Constitution.

questions.explanation: The Constitution fixes the existence of a Supreme Court, not its size. The tempting error is to treat statutory details as constitutional.
questions.hint: Existence is fixed, size is not.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The establishing decision on judicial review
questions.learningObjective: Identify the case establishing judicial review
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks which decision established judicial review of statutes.

options.text: Marbury v. Madison established judicial review.
McCulloch v. Maryland established judicial review.
Gibbons v. Ogden established judicial review.
Brown v. Board established judicial review.

questions.explanation: Marbury v. Madison established judicial review. The tempting error is to attribute review to a later or unrelated case.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks what judicial supremacy means for constitutional interpretation.

options.text: Judicial supremacy means only Congress interprets the Constitution.
Judicial supremacy eliminates executive enforcement discretion.
Judicial supremacy means courts have final say on constitutional meaning.
Judicial supremacy applies only to state courts.

questions.explanation: Judicial supremacy gives courts final say on constitutional meaning. The tempting error is to overstate it as eliminating other branches' roles.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log defines vertical stare decisis for new clerks.

answer.exemplar: Vertical stare decisis binds lower courts to follow the decisions of higher courts within the same jurisdiction, ensuring uniformity in the application of law.

questions.explanation: Vertical stare decisis binds lower courts to higher courts in the same jurisdiction. The tempting error is to confuse it with horizontal precedent.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A court generally follows its own prior decisions unless there is a compelling reason to overrule them. The dispatcher log must label this practice.

questions.stem: What is this practice called?

options.text: Vertical stare decisis.
Judicial restraint.
Judicial activism.
Horizontal stare decisis.

questions.explanation: A court following its own prior decisions is horizontal stare decisis. The tempting error is to confuse it with vertical precedent.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Duty of a lower court under precedent
questions.learningObjective: State a lower court's duty under precedent

stimulus.body: A lower court disagrees with a binding precedent from a higher court but must still apply it. The dispatcher log asks what duty applies.

questions.stem: What must the lower court do?

options.text: The lower court must follow the binding precedent.
The lower court may ignore the precedent it dislikes.
The lower court must certify the question upward first.
The lower court must overrule the precedent itself.

questions.explanation: Lower courts must follow binding precedent from higher courts. The tempting error is to assume disagreement frees them.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the role of circuit courts
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks what circuit courts primarily do.

options.text: Circuit courts are trial courts for minor cases.
Circuit courts only hear constitutional cases.
Circuit courts are intermediate appellate courts.
Circuit courts are state courts.

questions.explanation: Circuit courts are intermediate appellate courts. The tempting error is to confuse them with trial or state courts.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks which court has original jurisdiction in a dispute between two states.

options.text: No court has original jurisdiction in such disputes.
Only trial courts may hear state-versus-state disputes.
Appellate courts have original jurisdiction in all disputes.
The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction in state-versus-state disputes.

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction in disputes between states. The tempting error is to assume only trial courts hear cases first.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks why a plaintiff must show standing.

answer.exemplar: Standing is required to ensure the plaintiff has a concrete and particularised injury, preventing courts from issuing advisory opinions on abstract disputes.

questions.explanation: Standing requires a concrete, particularised injury to avoid advisory opinions. The tempting error is to allow suits by anyone with a general grievance.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A plaintiff sues before a threatened injury has actually materialised or become imminent. The dispatcher log must classify the barrier.

questions.stem: What doctrine bars this premature suit?

options.text: Mootness.
Standing.
Ripeness.
Exhaustion.

questions.explanation: Ripeness bars suits brought before an injury is imminent. The tempting error is to confuse it with mootness.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: The dispute has already resolved itself so no live controversy remains. The dispatcher log must classify the barrier.

questions.stem: What doctrine applies?

options.text: Ripeness.
Exhaustion.
Standing.
Mootness.

questions.explanation: Mootness bars suits when no live controversy remains. The tempting error is to confuse it with ripeness.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks why a plaintiff must exhaust administrative remedies first.

options.text: Exhaustion ensures agencies can resolve disputes before courts intervene.
Exhaustion lets courts rewrite agency rules.
Exhaustion eliminates the need for standing.
Exhaustion applies only to criminal cases.

questions.explanation: Exhaustion gives agencies a chance to resolve disputes first. The tempting error is to treat it as a way for courts to rewrite rules.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks when a court will decline a case as a political question.

options.text: When the issue involves foreign policy only.
When the issue is popular with voters.
When the issue is textually committed to another branch and lacks judicial standards.
When the issue is settled by statute.

questions.explanation: A political question arises when an issue is committed to another branch and lacks judicial standards. The tempting error is to treat any political topic as non-justiciable.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Resolve a conflict between a court order and a statute
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks how a court order interacts with a conflicting statute.

answer.exemplar: When a court order conflicts with a statute, the court order generally governs the parties before the court while the statute remains valid, subject to appeal or higher review.

questions.explanation: A court order governs the parties before the court even if it conflicts with a statute. The tempting error is to assume the statute automatically overrides the order.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A plaintiff challenges a law on both constitutional and statutory grounds. The dispatcher log must classify which issue reaches the Constitution.

questions.stem: Which issue is constitutional?

options.text: The claim that the law is unpopular.
The claim that the law conflicts with another statute.
The claim that the law is poorly drafted.
The claim that the law violates the First Amendment.

questions.explanation: A First Amendment challenge is constitutional, unlike statutory conflicts. The tempting error is to label any legal defect constitutional.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the scope of a remedy

stimulus.body: A court grants relief only to the named plaintiffs and does not extend it to similarly situated non-parties. The dispatcher log asks whether this is proper.

questions.stem: Is limiting relief to named plaintiffs proper?

options.text: No, relief must be nationwide in all cases.
No, relief must automatically cover all similarly situated persons.
Yes, relief is normally confined to the parties before the court.
Yes, but only in criminal cases.

questions.explanation: Relief is normally confined to the parties before the court. The tempting error is to assume remedies automatically extend to non-parties.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks what a consent decree is.

options.text: An executive order issued by the President.
A criminal sentence imposed after trial.
A legislative statute passed by Congress.
A court-approved settlement binding the parties.

questions.explanation: A consent decree is a court-approved settlement binding the parties. The tempting error is to confuse it with a sentence or statute.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Separation of powers as a design choice
questions.learningObjective: Apply separation of powers to a scenario
questions.stem: The dispatcher log notes a branch attempting to exercise another's core function.

options.text: This is permitted because branches may share any function.
This is required by checks and balances.
This raises separation-of-powers concerns.
This is allowed only in wartime.

questions.explanation: One branch exercising another's core function raises separation-of-powers concerns. The tempting error is to treat checks and balances as permission to usurp.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: The dispatcher log explains the dual court system to a new clerk.

answer.exemplar: The dual court system exists because federal courts resolve federal questions while state courts resolve state law, reflecting divided sovereignty and allowing parallel forums.

questions.explanation: Federal and state courts coexist under divided sovereignty. The tempting error is to assume one system handles all disputes.

Exhaustion.
Standing.
Mootness.

questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks why a plaintiff must exhaust administrative remedies first.

options.text: Exhaustion ensures agencies can resolve disputes before courts intervene.
Exhaustion lets courts rewrite agency rules.
Exhaustion eliminates the need for standing.
Exhaustion applies only to criminal cases.

questions.explanation: Exhaustion gives agencies a chance to resolve disputes first. The tempting error is to treat it as a way for courts to rewrite rules.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks when a court will decline a case as a political question.

options.text: When the issue involves foreign policy only.
When the issue is popular with voters.
When the issue is textually committed to another branch and lacks judicial standards.
When the issue is settled by statute.

questions.explanation: A political question arises when an issue is committed to another branch and lacks judicial standards. The tempting error is to treat any political topic as non-justiciable.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks how a court order interacts with a conflicting statute.

answer.exemplar: When a court order conflicts with a statute, the court order generally governs the parties before the court while the statute remains valid, subject to appeal or higher review.

questions.explanation: A court order governs the parties before the court even if it conflicts with a statute. The tempting error is to assume the statute automatically overrides the order.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A plaintiff challenges a law on both constitutional and statutory grounds. The dispatcher log must classify which issue reaches the Constitution.

questions.stem: Which issue is constitutional?

options.text: The claim that the law is unpopular.
The claim that the law conflicts with another statute.
The claim that the law is poorly drafted.
The claim that the law violates the First Amendment.

questions.explanation: A First Amendment challenge is constitutional, unlike statutory conflicts. The tempting error is to label any legal defect constitutional.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A court grants relief only to the named plaintiffs and does not extend it to similarly situated non-parties. The dispatcher log asks whether this is proper.

questions.stem: Is limiting relief to named plaintiffs proper?

options.text: No, relief must be nationwide in all cases.
No, relief must automatically cover all similarly situated persons.
Yes, relief is normally confined to the parties before the court.
Yes, but only in criminal cases.

questions.explanation: Relief is normally confined to the parties before the court. The tempting error is to assume remedies automatically extend to non-parties.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: The dispatcher log asks what a consent decree is.

options.text: An executive order issued by the President.
A criminal sentence imposed after trial.
A legislative statute passed by Congress.
A court-approved settlement binding the parties.

questions.explanation: A consent decree is a court-approved settlement binding the parties. The tempting error is to confuse it with a sentence or statute.
